chunk_findings.detail: The intent (and `_LISTS["research"] = "research notes with their verdicts"`) promises that `research list` shows verdicts, and the parallel callouts are all realized: `cmd_list` adds the `bug list` open-default and `_line` adds a `kind == "phase"` branch for `done`/`total`. There is no corresponding branch for `research`. `_line` builds every row from `id`, `state`, `title`, `owner`, `updated`; for `kind == "research"` it falls through to the generic format, so the verdict field (which the engine carries in the row, and which is present in `--json` output because `cmd_list` dumps `out.data` wholesale in the JSON path) is never rendered in the default text output. Concretely, running `ddflow research list` on a note whose row is `{"id": ..., "state": "open", "title": ..., "verdict": "supported", ...}` prints something like `  R-1                open       <title>  [@agent 2024-01-01]` with no `supported`/`refuted` anywhere, so the user cannot see the verdict the feature was added to surface. The phase column shows that a per-kind render branch was intended; the research one was omitted.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/commands/viewers_lists.py:_line

chunk_findings.detail: The change adds `research list` (confirmed by the same diff updating `tests/test_research_add.py` to expect the `{add,list}` help string), but the parity ledger only gains exemptions for `("task", "list")`, `("phase", "list")` and `("bug", "list")`. `("research", "list")` is not added. The parity test enumerates the CLI's (command, subcommand) pairs and fails on any pair that is neither mapped to an MCP tool nor listed in this exemption dict. Since the new `list` subcommand for research is a “read-only viewer over the shared list engine” with no MCP counterpart — exactly the rationale given for the other three additions — running `pytest tests/test_mcp_parity.py` will flag `("research", "list")` as uncovered and fail. The fix is to add the same exemption entry for `("research", "list")`.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_mcp_parity.py:~146 (the MCP parity exemption dict)

chunk_findings.detail: The test asserts that `research add --verdict CONFIRMED` fails with `--question`, but this does not actually prove the `add` subcommand exists. If the `add` subparser were removed and only the top-level `research` parser remained (the form used by the `proj` fixture), the same invocation would still fail with a missing-`--question` error because argparse checks required options before reporting the unexpected `add` token. So a regression that deletes the `add` subcommand goes undetected. Conversely, if the CLI really requires `research add`, the fixture’s bare `research --id R1 ...` invocation would fail, causing every test that depends on `proj` to error during setup. Either way the research CLI is not exercised consistently.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_view_cli_lists.py::test_research_add_still_requires_its_fields (and proj fixture)

chunk_findings.detail:
The change disables argparse's own enforcement (`for x in required: x.required = False`) and replaces it with a manual check that tests *truthiness* rather than *presence*:

```python
for x in required:
    if not getattr(a, x.dest):
        rs.error(f"the following arguments are required: {x.option_strings[0]}")
```

After `x.required = False`, this loop is the only enforcement of the required fields, and it is not equivalent to argparse's `required=True`, which only cares whether the option appeared on the command line. Two concrete divergences:

1. A supplied but falsy value is reported as missing. Any required option whose legitimate value is `0`, `""` or an empty list now fails. E.g. `ddflow research add --confidence 0 --title "..."` (or `--title ""` for a string field without `choices`) exits with `the following arguments are required: --confidence` even though the argument *was* supplied; the pre-change parser (`required=True`) accepted it, because argparse checks presence, not emptiness.
2. Conversely, a required option that happens to carry a non-empty `default` is no longer enforced at all: argparse with `required=True` still errors when the option is absent regardless of its default, but `not getattr(a, x.dest)` is `False` for that truthy default, so the wrapper silently proceeds.

The fix is to test presence explicitly (e.g. compare against the parser default / `argparse.SUPPRESS`, or track which dests were seen) rather than relying on truthiness.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/commands/viewers_lists.py (`register`, the `research` wrapper / required-argument re-check)

chunk_findings.detail: The stated intent adds a `list` subcommand to **four** CLIs — task, phase, bug and research — all "over the merged list engine (api view_list)" and all described identically as read-only viewers. This diff adds MCP-parity exemptions for only three of them: `("task", "list")`, `("phase", "list")`, and `("bug", "list")`, each with the rationale that the not-yet-existing consolidated `ddflow_list` MCP tool "will cover it, so it is exempt until then". The fourth, `("research", "list")`, is absent. Because the same reasoning applies verbatim to the research list viewer (it is the same engine and the consolidated MCP tool does not exist yet, so no MCP tool covers it either), the parity test will enumerate the newly registered `research list` CLI command, fail to find it in this exemption map, and fail to match it against any existing MCP tool. The concrete failure: run the parity test after wiring `research list`; it reports `("research", "list")` as an uncovered CLI command. (If the research list viewer were genuinely backed by an already-shipped MCP tool this would be moot, but the change's own intent says nothing of the sort — it lists research alongside the other three as an exempt-until-`dfllow_list` viewer.)

chunk_findings.detail: The `--limit` argument was changed from `default=V.DEFAULT_LIMIT` to `default=None`, with the default re-applied at call time via `a.limit or V.DEFAULT_LIMIT`. The `or` conflates an explicitly supplied `0` with "not given": for input `ddflow bug list --limit 0` (any list kind, e.g. `research list --limit 0`), argparse sets `a.limit == 0`, but `0 or V.DEFAULT_LIMIT` evaluates to `V.DEFAULT_LIMIT`, so the viewer silently shows `DEFAULT_LIMIT` rows instead. Before this change `a.limit` was forwarded as-is, so `--limit 0` reached the engine (where `0` is the conventional "no limit / show none" sentinel). The sentinel should be preserved with `limit=a.limit if a.limit is not None else V.DEFAULT_LIMIT`; as written, a user who explicitly asks for zero/unlimited rows gets a truncated listing with no error.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/commands/viewers_lists.py — `cmd_list`, `limit=a.limit or V.DEFAULT_LIMIT`

chunk_findings.detail: The test drives `--json task list --owner alice` and then asserts `json.loads(out)["filters"] == {"agent": "alice"}`. This change renames the list leaseholder filter to `--owner` precisely because `--agent` is now identity-only, so the applied list filter should be echoed under `owner`; hard-coding `agent` conflates the two names the change just split apart. Concretely: run `ddflow --json task list --owner alice`. If the implementation keys `filters` by the (renamed) option name, the output is `{"owner": "alice"}` and this assertion fails; if it really emits `{"agent": "alice"}`, then a JSON consumer looking at `filters.agent` cannot tell "the leaseholder filter I requested with --owner" from "my global identity", which is exactly the ambiguity the first half of this same test (`--agent alice` must show all 3 tasks) is trying to eliminate. Either the expected key should be `owner`, or the JSON `filters` payload must carry a distinct identity field — the assertion as written pins the wrong contract.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_view_cli_lists.py:113 (`test_the_global_agent_is_identity_not_a_filter`, final assertion)

chunk_findings.detail: Before this change the parser registered `--limit` with `default=V.DEFAULT_LIMIT` and `cmd_list` passed `a.limit` straight through, so `--limit 0` reached the engine as `0` (a request for zero rows). Now the parser default is `None` and the value is reconstructed with `a.limit or V.DEFAULT_LIMIT`; because `0` is falsy, an explicit `--limit 0` is silently rewritten to `V.DEFAULT_LIMIT`. Concretely, `ddflow bug list --limit 0` (or the same flag on `phase list` / `research list`) no longer returns an empty result but instead returns the default number of rows, i.e. the user's explicit argument is ignored. The correct reconstruction is `limit=V.DEFAULT_LIMIT if a.limit is None else a.limit`, which preserves an explicit zero while still substituting the default when the flag was omitted.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/commands/viewers_lists.py:87 (`limit=a.limit or V.DEFAULT_LIMIT` in `cmd_list`)

chunk_findings.detail: The intent says the leaseholder filter was renamed `--owner` precisely because `--agent` now denotes the global identity flag ("`--agent X` is identity"), and this very test is named to assert that `agent` is *not* a filter. Yet its last assertion, for the input `ddflow --json task list --owner alice`, expects `json.loads(out)["filters"] == {"agent": "alice"}` — i.e. the applied filter is echoed back under the pre-rename key `agent`. The test therefore contradicts its own premise: the machine-readable output reports the leaseholder filter using the exact key that the identity flag uses, so a JSON consumer cannot tell "the leaseholder filter `--owner alice` matched nothing" from "the identity flag `--agent alice` was set". Since the CLI flag is now `--owner`, the `filters` object should carry `owner` (e.g. `{"owner": "alice"}`); as written the expectation cements the stale key and hides the inconsistency.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_view_cli_lists.py::test_the_global_agent_is_identity_not_a_filter
